extracted.intended_audience: General readers, students, and researchers interested in the history of American radical magazines and early 20th‑century leftist/artistic periodicals
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic historical overview of the American radical magazine The Masses (1911–1917), describing its origins, editorial policy, contributors, art and literature, political positions, legal troubles, and legacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphical innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Masses was a graphically innovative American magazine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include cover illustrations (e.g., John French Sloan) and frequent use of illustrations and cartoons; the magazine employed techniques such as crayon sketches to capture rapid, on‑the‑spot feeling. Visual distinctiveness is highlighted as a defining feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Socialist politics / radical editorial orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Masses was an American magazine of socialist politics that published radical viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Published reportage, fiction, poetry and art by leading radicals; advocated labor causes, supported IWW and Eugene V. Debs, and criticized mainstream left publications for insufficient radicalism. Its political orientation shaped content selection and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication frequency and run
rubrics_metrics.description: Published monthly from 1911 until 1917.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dates and frequency are part of the magazine's factual production profile (first issue 1911; final issue 1917).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content mix: reportage, fiction, poetry, and art
rubrics_metrics.description: The magazine published a mix of reportage, fiction, poetry and art by prominent contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial practice favored a multidisciplinary mix — news reporting on labor struggles, creative literature (e.g., Sherwood Anderson), critical essays, and visual art — as part of its identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperative ownership and non‑profit editorial policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Owned and published cooperatively by its editors; 'It has no dividends to pay, and nobody is trying to make money out of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manifesto emphasizes a cooperative, noncommercial structure: 'A revolutionary and not a reform magazine... a magazine whose final policy is to do as it pleases and conciliate nobody.' This governance model informed editorial decisions and conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial stance: revolutionary, impertinent, and uncompromising
rubrics_metrics.description: Manifesto language: 'A revolutionary and not a reform magazine; a magazine with a sense of humour and no respect for the respectable; frank; arrogant; impertinent; searching for true causes; a magazine directed against rigidity and dogma... printing what is too naked or true for a money‑making press... conciliate nobody, not even its readers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone and mission are explicit criteria for content: provocative, satirical, uncompromising pieces were central. This is a normative editorial standard for what to publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association with Greenwich Village artistic culture
rubrics_metrics.description: The Masses was closely associated with New York's Greenwich Village artistic community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magazine's aesthetic and contributor base drew from the Village's artists and writers (Ashcan School, bohemian milieu), affecting subject matter, style, and contributor selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to Progressive Era reforms (e.g., women's suffrage, birth control)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Masses was more open to Progressive Era reforms like women's suffrage and birth control than some contemporary radical publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It advocated for birth control (supported activists like Margaret Sanger) and suffrage, sometimes controversially within Marxist circles; this editorial stance informed issue themes and critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti‑war content and denunciations of World War I
rubrics_metrics.description: After August 1914 the magazine's denouncements of the war were frequent and fierce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti‑war editorials and cartoons (e.g., Max Eastman's columns, Art Young's cartoons) constituted a sustained editorial line that later exposed the magazine to censorship and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efforts to comply with postal/Espionage Act regulations (mailing eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Masses attempted to comply with new regulations (Espionage Act) to remain eligible for shipment by the U.S. Post Office; business manager sought counsel to comply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural compliance (advising counsel, revising content) was necessary to access distribution channels; failure or perceived failure led to mail bans and practical suppression (excluded from mails, newsstands, Canadian mails, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal risk for content: criminal libel and charges under Espionage Act
rubrics_metrics.description: The magazine and its editors faced criminal libel suits (Associated Press) and Espionage Act charges for 'conspiring to obstruct conscription' and 'unlawfully and willfully…obstruct the recruiting and enlistment of the United States'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content with alleged suppression of facts, attacks on institutions (AP), or anti‑war advocacy could trigger prosecution; the article documents trials, indictments, and mistrials as consequences of editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial governance: cooperative board votes vs. single‑editor control
rubrics_metrics.description: Original vision was cooperative operation, but later Max Eastman's increased influence and publication of material without editorial‑board votes led to an artists' strike in 1916.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti‑pattern: moving toward 'one‑man magazine' rather than collaborative decision‑making. Practices like appending captions to artwork without artist consent sparked resignations; consultative editorial processes were presented as a standard to maintain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic standard: realist (Ashcan School) artwork and crayon technique
rubrics_metrics.description: For the most part the magazine published realist artwork associated with the Ashcan School, often using crayon technique to capture rapid sketches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations aimed to record real life and permit direct, unmediated responses to subjects. This aesthetic preference defined much visual content through circa 1916.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift toward modernist art in later years
rubrics_metrics.description: During later years the magazine embraced more modernist art (e.g., cover girls in modern attire), though it never dropped realist illustrations completely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates editorial evolution: a deliberate broadening of visual styles that could be judged as a change in editorial taste and positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of political cartoons as advocacy and provocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Political cartoons (notably by Art Young and Robert Minor) advocated socialist positions and were sometimes considered treasonous for anti‑war sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cartoons were an overt advocacy tool; their provocative nature both advanced the magazine's aims and increased legal/political vulnerability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage focus: labor struggles and industrial conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Masses reported on major labor struggles of its day (e.g., Paint Creek–Cabin Creek strike, Paterson silk strike, Ludlow Massacre) and sympathized with labor leaders and IWW.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commitment to in‑depth labor reportage and sympathy for union causes was a content selection criterion and part of the magazine's political identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for women's rights and sexual equality (including free love themes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The magazine vigorously argued for birth control and women's suffrage; some contributors promoted 'free love' in their pieces (sometimes veiled).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial willingness to publish contentious social views about sexuality and women's rights differentiated it from other socialist outlets and influenced reader and peer reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary criticism and discovery of new writers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Masses published literary criticism (e.g., Floyd Dell's 'Books that Are Interesting') and helped 'discover' writers (e.g., Sherwood Anderson) by publishing unsolicited manuscripts and supportive reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial practice included promoting American realism and new talent, sometimes without pay; this function served both literary and political goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial aim to combine revolutionary ideas with literature and art for their own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Max Eastman desired the magazine to combine revolutionary ideas with literature and art 'for its own sake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criterion stresses editorial balance between political advocacy and aesthetic/literary quality rather than purely propagandistic content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence and antagonism as a publishing principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The manifesto's insistence to 'do as it pleases and conciliate nobody, not even its readers' signals a normative principle of editorial independence and willingness to antagonize establishment and readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle justified provocative, nonconformist content and is presented as an intentional standard rather than an accidental trait.
